atoms.text: The crop share: a tenant pays the landlord half to two-thirds of the harvest, so labor is rewarded only after the owner takes their cut.
The company store: the landlord supplies food and tools on credit, so the worker's survival depends on the employer's ledger.
The crop lien: the year's harvest is collateral for a loan, so the future is mortgaged before it grows.
The debt that never clears: after the owner and merchant are paid, nothing remains, so labor reproduces its own bondage.
The tenant with a mule: a farmer who owns tools owes a smaller share, so autonomy is measured by equipment.
The landlord who provides everything: housing, seed, and animals come from the owner, so dependency is built into the contract.
The settlement day: the merchant sells the harvest on the worker's behalf and settles the debt, so the worker never touches the money.
The decentralized plot: scattered fields give the landlord no role, so the same institution can be intimate or absent.
The plantation store: long tenure ties a family to one owner, so the relationship outlasts individuals.
The salary that replaces the share: markets turn tenants into wage laborers, so one form of dependency becomes another.
The harvest festival: a community celebrates a crop it does not own, so joy and expropriation share a table.
The oral contract: the arrangement is traditional and legally governed, so memory and law compete over the terms.
The tenant who hides grain: a worker conceals part of the harvest to survive, so theft is the only form of savings.
The owner's generosity: a landlord forgives a debt and calls it kindness, so power is exercised through mercy.
The next generation's debt: children inherit the obligation to work the same land, so the contract is generational.
The record book: the owner's accounts determine who owes what, so truth is a private document.
